courseTitle: How IT Teams Work: Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban & Software Releases

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real, slightly vague feature request (e.g. 'the regional managers want a dashboard that updates automatically'). Decide, in writing, whether a Waterfall or Agile approach fits it better and justify the choice in 2-3 sentences the way the lesson contrasts a fixed-scope regulatory report against product work that will change as people react to it. Then write 3 real user stories for the request in the 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' shape, each with at least one checkable acceptance criterion.
slots.deliverable: A short written delivery-model recommendation (Agile or Waterfall, with justification) plus 3 user stories, each with an acceptance criterion.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a Kanban board (on paper or in a spreadsheet) with Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review, and Done columns, and place the 3 user stories from the previous slot into it, moving your top-priority story into To Do. Then, for that one story, write out what happens to it at each SDLC stage: what 'Dev' work looks like, what a QA tester would check before sign-off, what UAT sign-off from the business would say, and what changes once it reaches Production.
slots.deliverable: A Kanban board with 3 real stories placed in columns, plus a written Dev/QA/UAT/Production walkthrough for one of those stories.

slots.practicalActivity: In a real scratch Git repository (local or on GitHub), run the everyday workflow from the lesson end to end: clone, create and switch to a new branch, make a small change, add a .gitignore entry, commit with a specific message describing what changed and why, and push the branch. Open a pull request description summarizing the change for a reviewer. Then write one short, specific release note for that change in the 'Added: ... Known limitation: ...' style shown in the lesson, instead of a vague 'various improvements' note.
slots.deliverable: A real Git branch with at least one commit and a .gitignore entry, a pull request description, and one specific release note for the change.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for How Work Gets Done: take one new vague business request you write yourself, decide Agile vs. Waterfall, write 2 user stories with acceptance criteria, place them on a fresh Kanban board, and simulate pushing one of them through a Git branch/commit/PR cycle into a one-line release note -- connecting every concept from this chapter into one continuous flow before the capstone.
slots.deliverable: One consolidated practice packet: a model-choice decision, 2 user stories with acceptance criteria, a Kanban board, and a simulated Git branch-to-release-note flow for the same request.

slots.practicalActivity: Complete the Castlebridge Retail capstone from the lesson in full: write user stories (with acceptance criteria) for the revenue-by-region view, the revenue-by-category view, and the automatic daily refresh; build a Kanban board and place the stories on it; write a short QA test plan for one story that includes the zero-sales-region edge case; write a one-paragraph UAT sign-off in the sales director's voice; write a specific release note for the launch; and write up how you would investigate and communicate about the simulated production incident where a region's numbers show as zero two days after launch.
slots.deliverable: A complete capstone packet: 3 user stories with acceptance criteria, a Kanban board, a QA test plan covering the zero-sales edge case, a UAT sign-off, release notes, and a production-incident response write-up.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can read and participate in how a real IT team actually ships work -- choosing between Agile and Waterfall, writing testable user stories, tracking work on a Kanban board through Dev/QA/UAT/Production, using Git for version control, and writing a real release note -- the shared professional vocabulary every later course in the path assumes.
